title: Web performance and Core Web Vitals
subtitle: Measure how fast your pages feel to real users with LCP, INP and CLS, and fix the few things that matter most.

c.v: Vodafone had a landing page that people reached from paid ads: display, search, social, and iOS and Android. The team wanted to know if performance work alone would change sales.
. Half the traffic went to the old page and half to a faster one. The only difference was the Web Vitals work on the faster page. Each version got about 34,000 visits a day.

The faster page did three things. It moved a widget's rendering from the browser to the server, so less JavaScript blocked rendering. It rendered the important HTML on the server. And it resized the hero image, made SVGs and PNGs smaller, and did not load images outside the screen.
They measured real users with the browser's PerformanceObserver API.
dropped from 8.3 seconds to 5.7 seconds, 31% better. Total sales rose by 8%. The lead-to-visit rate rose by 15%, and the cart-to-visit rate by 11%.
If the team had watched only that number, they could have

Google chose the 75th percentile so that most visits get the target experience, while a few outliers do not move the number much.
Speed is three separate problems: loading, responding and staying still. Measure all three on real users, at the 75th percentile, and fix the biggest one first.

A long task that is already running makes the first phase long. A slow handler makes the second phase long.

c.v: Report LCP, INP and CLS at the 75th percentile, split by phone and desktop. Treat them like
Ask "which metric is bad, for which pages, on which devices?" before anyone writes a fix.
. The web.dev example is "less than 170 KB of JavaScript on mobile" for a product page. Tools like Lighthouse CI run checks on every commit to catch regressions.
Review every new third-party script like a dependency. Ask who owns it and what it costs on the main thread.
Check that the LCP image is in the HTML, not lazy, and sized for the screen.
When you show speed work to the business, use a real A/B test, like Vodafone did.
"Find the LCP element on our product page. Check that it is in the initial HTML, not lazy-loaded, has width and height, and uses fetchpriority=high. List what to change."

q.v: Which three metrics are the Core Web Vitals today?

why.v: INP replaced FID as a Core Web Vital in March 2024. TTFB is useful, but it is not a Core Web Vital.

q.v: Your field data shows LCP of 2.1 s at the median and 3.4 s at the 75th percentile, on phones. Does the page pass?

options.v: Yes, because the median is under 2.5 s.
No, because the 75th percentile is over 2.5 s.
It cannot be known without a Lighthouse score.

why.v: Google judges each metric at the 75th percentile of page loads. 3.4 s is above the 2.5 s good limit.

q.v: A Lighthouse run in your CI gives a perfect score, but real users report a slow page. What is the most likely reason?

options.v: Lab data uses one device and network and a cold cache, so it misses what real users get, including their taps.
Real users always have slower devices than any test can model, so field data cannot be trusted.

why.v: Lab data is repeatable but limited. Field data covers real devices, networks and interactions. Use both.

q.v: Users tap a filter button and the page freezes for half a second. Which fix targets the cause?

options.v: Add loading="lazy" to the hero image.
Break the long JavaScript task into smaller pieces and yield to the main thread.
Add a preconnect to the image CDN.

why.v: A long task on the main thread delays the response to input, which raises INP. Splitting it lets the browser handle the tap sooner.

q.v: Which change most directly lowers CLS?

options.v: Set width and height on images and reserve space for ads.
Lazy-load every image, including the hero.

why.v: Images and ads with unknown sizes push content down when they load. Reserving their space stops the move.
